title: Juju-chu!: The Jujutsu Guide for Agentic Coding
excerpt: A hands-on book on adopting Jujutsu (jj) with Claude Code and Codex: automatic snapshots, undoable operations, and safe history rewriting.
content_html:
The Jujutsu Guide for Agentic CodingLet your AI agents run wild. Undo anything, rewrite everything.

Jujutsu (jj) is a Git-compatible version control system with automatic snapshots, undoable operations, and safe history rewriting. This practical guide shows Git users how to experiment fearlessly, recover from anything, and turn AI-generated changes into clean, reviewable history.

Why This Book Exists

Two decades with Git. Then AI coding agents led me to Jujutsu.

For years, Git was the unquestioned foundation of my workflow. But when I started working daily with AI coding agents, the rhythm changed. Agents could generate, rewrite, and discard large amounts of code in minutes—while more and more of my time went into managing commits, recovering work through the reflog, and untangling history.

Then I found Jujutsu, a Git-compatible VCS built on a different model. Nothing was ever lost, nothing needed staging, and rewriting history stopped being something I braced myself for. For the first time in years, version control felt calm.

But learning individual commands was only half the story. I looked for a guide that showed how these ideas fit together into a real development workflow with AI agents. It didn’t exist yet—so I wrote it.

What You’ll Learn

  • Think in changes, not commits: the mental model that makes history editing feel natural
  • Undo anything with the operation log, no reflog archaeology required
  • Turn piles of AI-generated code into clean, reviewable history
  • Run parallel tasks—or parallel agents—with workspaces
  • Stop fearing merge conflicts: in jj, conflicts don’t block you
  • Ship your work to GitHub and collaborate with Git-based teams as usual

About The Style Of This Book

The dialogue isn’t decoration. It’s how the book teaches.

Juju-chu! unfolds as a conversation between two engineers: a senior who knows Jujutsu inside out, and a junior who keeps asking why.

The moment a question forms in your head—“but if you don’t control when commits happen, doesn’t your history end up chaotic?” “wait, if I rewrite past history, don’t I need to rebase?”—the junior asks it on the page. Misconceptions get corrected the moment they arise, and edge cases enter the discussion as objections, not footnotes.

It’s one of the oldest teaching devices there is—Socrates used it, and so does The Little Schemer. In Japan, it’s how my Riakuto! series reached 40,000 readers. Read the sample and see how it works.

Chapter Overview

Chapter 1

What Kind of Tool Is Jujutsu?

This chapter explores why Git’s human-paced model becomes a burden when AI agents make large, rapid changes. Staging gets skipped, context switches pile up, and rewriting history feels risky.

Then we introduce Jujutsu’s answer: automatic snapshots, universal undo, first-class conflicts, and consistent commands. You’ll see why Jujutsu lets you experiment first and clean up later.

Chapter 2

Let’s Try Jujutsu

After installation and setup, you’ll take a small project from initialization to GitHub—working with changes, reading history, and pushing your work. You’ll also meet Jujutsu’s three logs: the revision log, the evolution log for one change, and the operation log for the repository.

Then comes the mental model that makes everything else click: what a change is, how bookmarks differ from Git branches, and why working on anonymous branches becomes the default.

Chapter 3

Jujutsu × AI Workflow in Practice

This chapter shows how to steer Claude Code and Codex CLI toward jj instead of git, automate routine commands while keeping risky ones gated, and trigger formatting and linting through hooks.

Then comes a full workflow: turning an agent’s sprawling output into reviewable changes, pushing them for a PR, and running multiple agent sessions in parallel workspaces before merging their work back together.

Chapter 4

Advanced Jujutsu Techniques

Start with revsets and filesets—the query languages for selecting exactly the revisions and files you mean—then meet three power-user commands: jj absorb, which sends fixes back to the changes they belong to, jj arrange, and jj bookmark advance.

From there, you’ll build a custom jj push for pre-push checks, reduce manual conflict resolution with Mergiraf and Weave, and explore UI tools including jjui and JJ View.

Chapter 5

The Jujutsu Problem-Solving Guide

The FAQ answers the questions Git users keep asking: why there’s no pull command, how to do the equivalent of cherry-pick, how to keep temporary files out of your history, and whether Jujutsu is really just a wrapper around Git.

Then come the problems that stop you cold—a plain push that silently becomes a force push, a stale working copy, a change that picked up a divergent annotation, and working-copy commit wandering off after you merge a PR and fetch the result.

Free config files: make your AI agent use Jujutsu instead of Git

Who This Book Is For (And Who It Isn’t)

You’ll get the most out of Juju-chu! if:

  • Your AI agent writes most of your code, and Git’s three-state workflow keeps creating friction—or has already caused you to lose uncommitted work.
  • You’ve lost AI-generated work—never committed before the next prompt, wiped by a stray git reset --hard, or destroyed by a Git command the agent ran on its own.
  • Splitting massive AI code dumps into clean, reviewable, and logical changes feels like a tedious chore.
  • You still hold your breath during a Git rebase, constantly worried about breaking history or losing context.
  • You’re curious about Jujutsu, but want a practical blueprint for daily agentic development—not just abstract concepts or a list of commands.

This book is probably not for you if:

  • You are completely new to Git and GitHub. This book assumes familiarity with Git; it’s designed to help you move beyond it.
  • You wield reflog and interactive rebase with absolute confidence, and feel your Git workflow has zero friction.
  • You don’t use AI coding agents at all. The book is built around an AI-first development workflow.

About The Author

Written by Yuka Ooka

Yuka Ooka is a Japanese technical author whose React + TypeScript series Riakuto! (りあクト！) has sold more than 40,000 copies.

She began her career as a PHP and Ruby developer and product manager before going freelance in 2016. An early adopter of React in Japan, she later worked with clients as a React specialist.

Her latest book, Juju-chu!, is the first comprehensive guide to the Jujutsu version control system—and to pairing it with AI coding agents like Claude Code.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need any prior experience with Jujutsu?

No. The book starts with installation and builds up from there—no prior familiarity assumed. Kanae, the junior engineer in the dialogue, has never touched Jujutsu either, so you learn alongside her.

That said, it’s not only for complete newcomers to Jujutsu. If you’ve tried it before and bounced off the gap between Git’s mental model and Jujutsu’s, the book spends real time closing that gap: what a change really is, why commit IDs change while change IDs stay put, and where your Git instincts will mislead you.

Do I need to know Git?

Yes—this is the one prerequisite. Juju-chu! assumes you’ve used Git day to day: cloning, branching, committing, pushing, and opening pull requests. Much of the book explains Jujutsu by contrasting it with Git, so those comparisons only land if Git already feels familiar.

What you don’t need is Git mastery. If reflog is a mystery to you and interactive rebase makes you nervous, you’re exactly who this book was written for.

Do I have to make my whole team switch from Git?

No. Jujutsu works directly with an existing Git repository, so you can adopt it on an existing project without touching anyone else’s setup. What you push to GitHub is ordinary Git commits—your teammates keep using Git, review your pull requests as usual, and never need to know you switched.

That makes Jujutsu unusually low-risk to try: the decision is yours alone, and it’s reversible. Git is still right there underneath, so you can switch back to git commands anytime.

Do I need Claude Code or Codex?

No. The book uses Claude Code and Codex CLI as its worked examples, but nothing about the Jujutsu side is specific to either one.

The Codex setup is built on AGENTS.md and skills—open conventions that Cursor, OpenCode, and other agents also read. So the rules and instructions in the book carry over with little more than a change of filename. What you’re really learning is how to teach an agent to use Jujutsu instead of Git, and that carries over from tool to tool.

Which version of Jujutsu does the book cover?

Jujutsu v0.43.0, released in July 2026. Every command and every log output in the book comes from an actual run against that version—nothing is written from memory or reconstructed by hand.

Jujutsu is still pre-1.0 and moves quickly, so some details will inevitably shift. But the book concentrates on the model underneath: what a change is, how the working copy is committed for you, and why history can be rewritten safely. That model is the book’s real subject—not a frozen snapshot of the CLI—and it’s the part that’s hardest to pick up from release notes.

Will the book be updated?

Yes, within limits. If a breaking change in Jujutsu makes the book’s existing instructions inaccurate, I’ll revise the affected sections. I’ll also fix errors and clarify anything that could be explained better.

This is a finished book, not a continuously expanding reference. Updates will focus on keeping the existing material accurate—not covering every new Jujutsu feature or substantially reorganizing the book.

Leanpub readers get these updates at no extra charge. Updated Kindle files may also be published, though whether Amazon pushes them to existing customers is out of my hands; you can usually pull the latest version yourself from Manage Your Content and Devices.

Which edition is right for me?

PDF and EPUB (Leanpub)—carefully typeset with embedded fonts and completely DRM-free. The PDF preserves the full page design, while the EPUB reflows for smaller screens without sacrificing the book’s typography. If you care about how a technical book looks and reads, or you want to keep the files somewhere Amazon can’t reach, this is the one.

Kindle (Amazon)—the right pick if your reading life already lives in the Kindle app. The text reflows to fit your device, though some of the original typography is inevitably lost.

Paperback (Amazon)—6 × 9 inches, 163 pages, and the only way to get Juju-chu! in print.

Readers have also asked which purchase supports me more directly. I keep a slightly larger share of a Leanpub sale than a Kindle sale. The digital editions are the same price, so buy wherever suits you—but if it’s a coin flip, that’s the tiebreaker.
